docs.text: Changelog All notable changes to wikicc are documented in this file. The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning. Entries describe what a user of the binary can observe, not how the change was implemented; the rules behind them live in docs/design.md. [2.2.0] - 2026-11-17 Builds run in parallel across the machine's cores, a front matter title can name the document, and a sealed document carries its assets with it. Added Parallel compilation. The per-document work — rendering each document's Markdown, resolving its links and assets, sealing the documents marked encrypt — runs across the machine's cores and is merged in scan order, so the worker count changes how long a build takes, never the bytes. --jobs N caps the worker threads (--jobs 1 keeps the parallel stages effectively sequential); the setting takes the same three sources as every other one — --jobs over WIKICC_JOBS over the configuration file's jobs key — and without any of them the build uses every available core. A value below 1 fails the build. A front matter title names the document wherever the reader shows a title — the sidebar, the link graph, search, the lock page and the browser tab — while the body keeps its headings. Numbers and booleans are read as text; a value that cannot become a title warns at build time and the first heading (else the file name) decides. The payload the reader loads carries a format version, and the reader refuses a payload whose version it does not know. Fixed Assets a sealed document references are expanded into data URIs before sealing, so images inside encrypted documents render in the single file, and assets used only by sealed documents are pruned from the site. [2.1.0] - 2026-11-16 A document can be sealed with a password, settings can come from environment variables, and the reader frame is rebuilt around two slim rails with a floating link-graph window. Added Document encryption. An encrypt field in a document's front matter (true for the global password, or a password of its own) seals the body with AES-256-GCM at build time. The password comes from --password, the WIKICC_PASSWORD variable, or the configuration file; building an encrypted document without a password available is an error naming the document. A locked document keeps its title visible in the sidebar and in search; the reader shows a locked page with an unlock form in place of the article, and the unlocked body is kept in memory for the session only — it is never written to storage. Environment variables as a settings source. Every option the command line and .wikicc.json accept is also spelled as a WIKICC_-prefixed variable (WIKICC_OUT, WIKICC_FORMAT, WIKICC_TITLE, WIKICC_STRICT, WIKICC_HOME, WIKICC_EXCLUDE, WIKICC_FAVICON, WIKICC_PASSWORD), read below the command line and above the file. A blank variable did not speak, an unknown WIKICC_* name is ignored, and a value that cannot be understood fails the build naming the variable. A favicon for the reader page: the project logo is embedded as the default, and --favicon, the favicon configuration key, or WIKICC_FAVICON points at a different file. Every code block in the article carries a copy button, and a successful copy is announced with a check. The link preview popover grows edge handles and can be resized from its borders. A link to another web page opens in a new tab. The document sidebar can be hidden and shown again at desktop widths; on phone widths it stays a drawer. The link graph is split into a local and a global panel — the current document's neighbourhood and the whole folder — each opened from its own switch on the right rail. On desktop widths the panel floats above the article as a window, so opening or closing it no longer shifts the layout. Changed The reader frame is rebuilt around two slim rails: the left one switches the sidebar between the document list and the chapter outline, the right one carries search, the theme switch and the link-graph switches. The top toolbar is gone. The link preview panel opens on the roomier side of the article, so it never covers the link it previews. Fixed Syntax highlighting in the light theme keeps its colours instead of washing out. A table keeps the column widths it was laid out with, so sorting and filtering no longer shift them. [2.0.1] - 2026-11-09 Fixed Search results and their preview agree: the list is built in reading order, so a hit inside a code block opens at that very block, and the selected row always points at the passage the preview shows. A search hit marks the typed fragment only instead of widening to the whole word: searching read marks read in reader rather than the word. The number of hits is unchanged. Changed A search result's context line is cut to the width the row really has, so wide characters such as CJK no longer overflow it or end it early; the line follows the panel width and the font size as they change. [2.0.0] - 2026-11-06 Second release: search becomes a panel with previews, math is typeset, links preview on hover, chapters fold, and a site can be built as a static pages artifact configured by a .wikicc.json. Added A search panel replaces the sidebar search field. It searches the current document (local) or the whole folder (global), lists one row per occurrence with a one-line context, and previews the passage with every hit marked, including hits inside inline code. Enter opens a result at its place in the article; the arrow keys keep the selected row in sight and survive a scope switch. Math typesetting: inline $…$ and block $$…$$ formulas are rendered with the bundled KaTeX, offline like everything else. Hover previews cover whole documents: a link to another document previews the document, a link to one of its chapters previews that chapter. A preview opens at once with a loading state; when it cannot be built, the panel shows a failure notice with a retry instead of closing. Scrolling inside the preview never scrolls the article underneath. Chapter folding: an arrow beside a heading folds that chapter — and everything nested under it — down to its title, and unfolds it again. The arrows appear when the pointer is on a heading, and folding is never remembered. The pages output format: a static site for an HTTP host such as GitHub Pages. The page carries the reader and a manifest only; each document is a JSON chunk fetched on navigation, and the global search corpus is fetched on first use, so first paint does not grow with the size of the folder. An optional .wikicc.json in the input folder root configures the opening document (home), excluded directories (exclude), the output directory (out), the format, the title and strict; every command-line flag overrides the file. wikicc --init-config writes a starter file without overwriting. --exclude keeps directories out of the site from the command line. Inlined data: asset links open as blob URLs in a new tab. The link graph can switch between the whole folder (global) and the current document's neighbourhood (local). Destinations of inline images and links may contain spaces. Changed Multi-character CJK queries match consecutive text only: the characters of a query no longer scatter across the document as separate hits. The search preview shows the passage alone, without a title and path banner, and centers the picked hit. The link graph is tighter: the frame adapts to the content, and nodes and labels are smaller. Release archives are named after the system that built them and the architecture: wikicc-ubuntu-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.tar.gz and wikicc-windows-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.zip. Fixed Reference-style links no longer silently degrade to plain text in citation-dense documents. The search preview lands on the right passage after a hit inside a code block. The search field shows a single clear button: the browser's native clear cross is hidden. The reader's bundled JavaScript and CSS are normalized to LF at build time, so two builds of one input stay byte-identical whatever the checkout's line endings. [1.0.0] - 2026-11-03 First stable release: the features the reader offers. Reader Compile a folder of Markdown documents into a self-contained reader that needs no server, no sibling files and no network. Search over titles, headings and body text, including CJK. Link graph of the folder with zoom, pan and drag; a plain left click opens the document of the node. Chapter outline of the current document, following the section being read. Block references: pointing at a chapter of another document previews that chapter, and the preview can be pinned and dragged out of the way. A chapter that does not exist is reported as a broken reference and explained. Tables with sorting and Excel-style per-column filtering. Light and dark themes, and a layout that stays usable down to phone width. Markdown support GitHub-flavored Markdown: tables, task lists, strikethrough and footnotes. Nested chapters with stable, Unicode-aware heading anchors, so CJK headings keep their text. Chapter links that address one chapter of another document ([label](doc.md#chapter)) or the document as a whole. Reference-style links ([[n]] plus a reference list) alongside ordinary Markdown links, and a reference list rendered for the styles that use it. Fenced code highlighting, done at build time. Mermaid diagrams from a fence tagged mermaid. Raw HTML inside Markdown, passed through unchanged; the input is trusted, so untrusted documents must not be compiled. Output Two output formats: single-html (one page with everything inlined, opens by double click from any directory) and html-dir (a page plus an assets/ folder, ready to be copied, zipped or served as it is). Assets addressed by content, so identical bytes are stored once no matter how many documents reference them. Nothing is fetched at runtime: no CDN, no web font, no remote stylesheet. Two builds of the same input produce byte-identical artifacts. Executable One binary with no runtime dependencies: on Windows it carries the project logo as an icon in the file explorer. Statically linked release archives for Linux and Windows, so neither needs runtime packages on the machine that runs it.

docs.text: wikicc Compile a folder of Markdown documents into a self-contained, offline HTML reader you can double-click. The compiled reader needs no server, no sibling files and no network: search the whole folder, read a document with syntax highlighting and Mermaid diagrams, follow the link graph between documents, and navigate long documents through their chapter outline. Features Reader Search over titles, headings and body text, including CJK. Link graph of the folder with zoom, pan and drag; clicking a node opens that document. Chapter outline of the current document, following the section being read. Chapter folding: an arrow beside a heading folds that chapter — and everything nested under it — down to its title, and unfolds it again. The arrows appear when the pointer is on a heading and stay out of the way otherwise; folding is never remembered, so every document opens whole. Following a link or an outline entry into a folded chapter reopens it. Block references: a link to a chapter of another document previews that chapter on hover and opens it on click, and a link to a whole document previews that document on hover. A chapter that does not exist is reported as a broken reference and explained by the reader. Tables: sorting and Excel-style per-column filtering. Filtering never shifts the column widths: they are measured at the last layout-affecting moment — the page loading, the window being resized — and pinned until the next one. Code blocks: a button on every code block copies its text to the clipboard; inline code, diagrams and formulas are left alone. Content viewer: hovering a rendered diagram frames it and shows one button that lifts the picture into a large lightbox, where it can be zoomed, panned and reset to its fitted state; Escape, the backdrop or the close button put it away. The viewer is built to carry other kinds of content later, each with actions of its own. Theme toggle (light/dark) and a layout that stays usable down to phone width. Markdown support GitHub-flavored Markdown: tables, task lists, strikethrough and footnotes. Front matter title: a title key in the front matter names the document wherever the reader shows a title — the sidebar, the link graph, search, the lock page and the browser tab — while the body keeps its headings. Numbers and booleans are read as text; a value that cannot become a title warns at build time and the first heading (else the file name) decides. Nested chapters with stable, Unicode-aware heading anchors, so CJK headings keep their text. Chapter links: [label](path/to/doc.md#chapter) addresses one chapter of another document, [label](path/to/doc.md) addresses the document as a whole. Images and other local assets: ![alt](path/to/image.png) is embedded content-addressed, and a destination containing spaces is accepted too. Fenced code highlighting, done at build time. Mermaid diagrams from a fence tagged mermaid. Raw HTML inside Markdown, passed through unchanged. The input is trusted: there is no sanitizer, so do not compile untrusted documents. Encrypted documents A document whose front matter declares encrypt is sealed into the artifact: AES-256-GCM ciphertext, so a copied artifact shows no body, no chapter structure and no password. The reader unlocks it in place, the title stays public and searchable, and unlocked passwords live in the session's memory alone. See docs/encrypt.md for the full contract. Output formats Format Artifact Assets single-html (default; one self-contained file) one index.html inlined into the page html-dir (page plus an assets folder) index.html + assets/ one file per unique resource pages (static site for GitHub Pages) index.html + pages/ + search.json + assets/ one file per unique resource All three carry the same reader. Assets are content-addressed, so identical bytes are stored once no matter how many documents reference them. single-html opens by double click, offline, from any directory, with no sibling files. html-dir is smallest and can be copied, zipped or served statically as it is. pages is a static site for an HTTP host such as GitHub Pages: the page carries the reader and a document manifest only, and each document's content is one JSON file under pages/ that the reader fetches when it navigates there. The search corpus is a separate search.json, fetched the first time the reader searches the whole site. Nothing but the shell and the manifest is downloaded up front, so first paint does not grow with the size of the folder. This format needs to be served over HTTP(S) — a browser refuses the fetches from a file:// page, and the reader says so when it finds itself there. Publishing to GitHub Pages pages output deploys as it is: hash routes need no server configuration, the file names are stable across builds (a cached page never points at a file a redeploy removed), and each fetch carries the content hash of the chunk it wants, so a browser that still holds a cached page refreshes its documents after a redeploy. The artifact works at the root of a domain and under a subpath alike: wikicc path/to/docs --format pages -o site git -C path/to/docs add site && git -C path/to/docs commit -m "Publish" git -C path/to/docs subtree push --prefix site origin gh-pages Offline and reproducibility The shell formats fetch nothing at runtime: no CDN, no web font, no remote stylesheet. pages fetches only the files the build wrote next to the page — never a third-party origin. The build itself never touches the network; the only network step is the one-time npm ci that installs the pinned front-end dependencies. Two builds of the same input produce byte-identical artifacts, in every format. Usage Prerequisites and install Rust 1.85 or newer (the crate uses edition 2024). Node.js 22.12 or newer and npm — the reader is bundled at build time, and 22.12 is the floor of the diagram engine. Node is needed for the build and the quality tooling: build.rs runs the native esbuild executable of the @esbuild/<os>-<cpu> package directly, and the formatter and linter of the front-end sources are installed into the same node_modules. npm ci # once, and again whenever package-lock.json changes cargo build --release # build.rs bundles the reader into the binary cargo install --path . # optional: put `wikicc` on PATH The compiled binary and the generated HTML have no external dependencies. Prebuilt binaries The releases page carries the binaries CI builds for each tagged version, one archive per build system and architecture: Build system Architecture Archive Binary inside Ubuntu amd64 wikicc-ubuntu-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.tar.gz wikicc Windows amd64 wikicc-windows-amd64-v<version>-<sha>.zip wikicc.exe The archive name states the system it was built on rather than the kernel it runs on, so the same archive also tells you which CI image produced it. Unpack it anywhere and put the binary on PATH; nothing else has to be installed. The Ubuntu binary is statically linked against musl, so it runs on any distribution without a matching glibc, and the Windows executable links the C runtime statically, so it does not need the VC++ redistributable. Command line wikicc [OPTIONS] [INPUT_DIR] [INPUT_DIR] Folder that contains the Markdown documents; defaults to the current directory -o, --out <DIR> Output directory [default: <INPUT_DIR>/dist] --format <FMT> single-html | html-dir | pages [default: single-html] --title <TITLE> Site title [default: input folder name] --strict[=<BOOL>] Treat warnings as errors; --strict=false turns the gate off --home <DOC> Document the reader opens first; overrides .wikicc.json --exclude <DIR> Directory to keep out of the site; repeatable, overrides .wikicc.json --favicon <FILE> Favicon file relative to the input folder; overrides .wikicc.json [default: the wikicc logo] --password <PASSWORD> Global password for documents whose front matter declares encryption; overrides .wikicc.json. Prefer the WIKICC_PASSWORD environment variable: a command line value stays in the shell history and the process list -j, --jobs <N> Worker threads the parallel build stages may use; overrides .wikicc.json [default: all cores] --force Overwrite the output directory without confirmation -q, --quiet Suppress the summary line --init-config [DIR] Write a default .wikicc.json into DIR [default: the current directory] and exit -h, --help Print help -V, --version Print version wikicc path/to/docs # writes path/to/docs/dist/index.html wikicc path/to/docs -o build --title "Handbook" wikicc path/to/docs --format html-dir wikicc path/to/docs --format pages # a static site for GitHub Pages wikicc path/to/docs --strict # broken links fail the build wikicc path/to/docs --home guide/intro.md # override the configured opening document wikicc path/to/docs --exclude drafts # override the configured exclusions wikicc path/to/docs --favicon assets/icon.png WIKICC_PASSWORD="opensesame" wikicc path/to/docs # seal documents marked encrypt: true wikicc path/to/docs --password "opensesame" # the same seal, but the password lands in the shell history wikicc path/to/docs --jobs 4 # cap the parallel build at four worker threads wikicc --init-config path/to/docs # writes path/to/docs/.wikicc.json A successful build prints a summary line and reports diagnostics on stderr; --quiet suppresses the summary only. Environment variables Every setting can also come from a WIKICC_* environment variable, spelled in upper case. The command line overrides the variables; the variables override .wikicc.json. Variable Meaning WIKICC_OUT Output directory; relative to the working directory, like --out WIKICC_FORMAT single-html, html-dir or pages WIKICC_TITLE Site title WIKICC_STRICT Fail the build on warnings; true, false, 1 or 0 WIKICC_HOME Document the reader opens first WIKICC_EXCLUDE Comma-separated directories kept out of the site WIKICC_FAVICON Favicon file relative to the input folder WIKICC_PASSWORD Global password for documents whose front matter declares encryption WIKICC_JOBS Worker threads the parallel build stages may use; a positive integer A variable that is not set, or whose value is blank, did not speak: the next source down decides. A value that cannot be understood — an unknown format, an unparseable boolean, an empty exclusion entry — fails the build with an error naming the variable. Only the nine names above count; any other WIKICC_* variable in the environment is ignored, because that namespace belongs to other programs too. --force, --quiet, --init-config and the input directory exist only on the command line, never as variables. Output directory A missing directory is created; an empty one is used as it is. A directory holding a previous build is emptied and reused, so rebuilding needs no flags and leaves no stale files. Any other non-empty directory requires --force. The output directory cannot be the input folder, an ancestor of it, or the current working directory, and it is excluded from scanning. Symlinks inside the output directory are removed as links, never followed. Configuration file A site can carry an optional .wikicc.json in the input folder root. The file is JSON and knows keys — the same settings the command line and the WIKICC_* environment variables take, so each of them can also be overridden by a flag or a set variable: Key Meaning home Document the reader opens at an empty or unknown address [default: the first document] exclude Directories whose entire subtrees stay out of the site [default: none] out Output directory [default: <INPUT_DIR>/dist] format single-html, html-dir or pages [default: single-html] title Site title [default: the input folder name] favicon Favicon file relative to the input folder [default: the wikicc logo] password Global password for documents whose front matter declares encryption; read verbatim strict Fail the build on warnings [default: false] jobs Worker threads the parallel build stages may use, at least 1 [default: all cores] home is a document id — the path relative to the input folder, / separated, extension included — and a missing .md (or .markdown) suffix is completed, so "home": "intro" addresses intro.md. Explicit links are never redirected: the setting only decides what the opening page shows, and the sidebar, graph and search see the same document they always did. exclude lists directories relative to the input folder; each pruned directory takes its documents and subfolders with it, so drafts and private notes never reach the payload, the search index or the link graph. Entries are normalized like home values — trimmed, \ read as /, a leading ./ and a trailing / dropped — and match exactly: "drafts" prunes the input folder's own drafts directory, not guide/drafts. The build reports how many directories were pruned as a note line. out is resolved against the input folder — the directory the configuration file sits in — so a relative value builds to the same place no matter which working directory the build was started from. A command line --out keeps its own convention: relative to the working directory. So does WIKICC_OUT — the variable speaks from the shell or CI job that exports it. favicon is a file path relative to the input folder (\ is read as /, a leading ./ is dropped; an absolute path is taken as it is). Every page carries it as its <link rel="icon">: the icon travels through the same content-addressed asset system as the documents' images, inlined as a data URI by single-html and written to assets/ by the other two formats. Without the key the reader carries the wikicc logo, which is embedded into the executable at build time. { "home": "guide/getting-started.md", "exclude": ["drafts", "archive/old"], "out": "site", "format": "pages", "title": "Handbook", "favicon": "assets/icon.png", "password": "opensesame", "strict": false, "jobs": 4 } Every value the file names is a default; a set WIKICC_* variable wins over it, and an explicit flag wins over the variable. WIKICC_OUT, WIKICC_FORMAT, WIKICC_TITLE, WIKICC_STRICT, WIKICC_HOME, WIKICC_EXCLUDE, WIKICC_FAVICON, WIKICC_PASSWORD and WIKICC_JOBS override their configured counterparts; the command line flags below override the variables again. --home replaces the configured home. --exclude replaces the configured list entirely; repeat the flag for several directories. --out, --format, --title, --favicon, --password and --jobs override their configured counterparts. A bare --strict turns the gate on and --strict=false turns it off, whatever the file says. --force and --quiet exist only on the command line; the file never asks for a destructive overwrite or a silent build. A home that matches no document is a warning — the build still succeeds and the reader falls back to the first document; --strict turns it into a failure. An exclude entry that escapes the input folder (..) or cannot match any directory (empty) fails the build for the same reason a broken home would, whatever the source it came from. A favicon that is empty after normalization or escapes the input folder fails the build the same way, and a configured favicon file that cannot be read fails the build too: the icon is an explicit instruction, not something to silently replace with the default. An unreadable or invalid file fails the build: a broken instruction must not be silently ignored. Unknown keys warn, so a typo never silently changes nothing. Every output format honours the settings, and a site without a .wikicc.json builds exactly the artifact it always did. A starter file can be written with wikicc --init-config [DIR] (the current directory when the value is omitted). It writes the default content — every key unset: { "home": null, "exclude": null, "out": null, "format": null, "title": null, "favicon": null, "password": null, "strict": null, "jobs": null } The target directory must already exist; a missing directory is rejected, not created. An existing .wikicc.json is never overwritten — delete it first. --init-config cannot be combined with an input directory. Encrypted documents A document's front matter can ask the build to seal it: encrypt: true seals it with the global password, encrypt: "secret" seals it with a password of its own, and a missing key, false or null builds the document as usual — every other value fails the build with an error naming the document. The global password takes the same three sources as every setting — --password over WIKICC_PASSWORD over the configuration file's password key — and a sealed declaration that finds no password anywhere fails the build with exit code 1 and nothing written, whatever --strict says. The title stays public; the full contract — marking, password sources, the reader's lock page and the scheme's boundaries — is described in docs/encrypt.md. Parallel compilation The per-document work — parsing and rendering every document's Markdown, resolving its links and assets, and sealing the documents marked encrypt — runs in parallel across the machine's cores. The results are collected and merged in the scan order, so the thread count changes how long a build takes, never the bytes: two builds of the same input are byte-identical whatever the worker count was. --jobs N caps the worker threads (--jobs 1 keeps the parallel stages effectively sequential — the knob for comparing a suspicious artifact against a known-good one). The setting takes the same three sources as every other one — --jobs over WIKICC_JOBS over the configuration file's jobs key — and without any of them the build uses every available core. A value below 1 fails the build with exit code 1. Warnings and --strict Broken links, missing assets, chapter anchors a document does not have and links that escape the input directory are warnings: the build still succeeds and the original destination is left untouched, so the reader can still show the link. --strict turns warnings into a failure. The gate runs before anything is written, so a refused build neither creates an artifact nor empties a previous one. Exit codes Code Meaning 0 Success (possibly with warnings) 1 Runtime failure: missing input, I/O error, --strict with warnings, a sealed document without a password 2 Usage error: invalid arguments Documentation CHANGELOG.md — what changed in each release. docs/search.md — how the reader's search works, and the query syntax it understands. docs/encrypt.md — how sealed documents work: marking them, passwords, the reader's lock page and the scheme's boundaries. docs/design.md — how wikicc is built. docs/CONTRIBUTING.md — the development rules: the quality gates every commit has to pass, and the steps that regenerate the Windows icon. tests/README.md — how the test suite is organised. Development See docs/CONTRIBUTING.md. License GPL-3.0-only. See LICENSE for the full text.

docs.text: wikicc — Development rules These rules bind every commit, not just the ones that change behaviour. They are kept here rather than in README.md so that the product description stays a description of the product: the architecture lives in design.md, the test suite in ../tests/README.md, and the obligations a change has to meet live in this document. Quality gates Every commit is expected to leave the quality gates green, and every one of the four has to run locally before committing: a subset — one integration file, only the unit tests, only the front-end suite — does not clear the bar. cargo fmt --check # Rust formatting cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings # Rust lint npm run check # JS formatting and lint (Biome) cargo test # everything, including the front-end suite npm run check covers the reader's own JavaScript — the modules in src/web/js, the tests in tests/js and the scripts in tools, as scoped by biome.jsonc — and fails on a formatting difference, a lint violation or a lint warning; third-party code under node_modules is never touched. npm run format rewrites the formatting in place and npm run lint runs only the lint half. The gates and the suite they protect are described further in ../tests/README.md. A gate that has to be skipped is a reason not to commit, not a reason to commit with a warning. The Windows icon docs/logo.svg is the design source of the executable icon; docs/logo.ico is a derived asset, rendered from it and committed, so that the build needs no image toolchain. After changing the design source, the icon has to be rendered again: Render docs/logo.svg to square PNGs named logo-<size>.png, with <size> in 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 128 and 256. Any renderer will do; the sizes have to match exactly. Pack them into the icon: node tools/make-icon.mjs <png-dir> docs/logo.ico Rebuild. tools/make-icon.mjs refuses a PNG whose size does not match its name, so an incomplete set is caught before the icon is written. The source and the derived asset must never be committed out of step: a change to docs/logo.svg carries the regenerated docs/logo.ico in the same commit.

docs.headings: wikicc — Architecture 1. Shape of the system 2. Pipeline 3. Module map 4. Invariants 5. Determinism 6. Contracts at the edges 7. Front end 8. Article encryption 9. Testing 10. Constraints and risks
docs.text: wikicc — Architecture This document describes how wikicc is built: its layers, the direction of their dependencies, the invariants the stages must keep, and the constraints that shape them. It deliberately stays at that level — product behaviour is described in README.md, the encryption scheme in docs/encrypt.md, and per-stage implementation details live in the code. 1. Shape of the system wikicc is one Rust binary plus one embedded front-end bundle. The binary owns everything that can be decided at build time; the bundle owns everything that has to happen in the reader. They communicate through exactly one channel: a JSON payload embedded in the page. build time │ run time │ input dir ──▶ pipeline stages ──▶ artifact │ artifact ──▶ reader modules (Rust: scan, parse, resolve, │ (ES modules bundled by assemble, render, write) │ esbuild, inlined as one │ classic script) payload (JSON) ─┼─▶ Nothing is resolved at run time across the boundary: the bundle knows its imports when it is built, and the payload is already on the page when the script runs. There is no server in either half. 2. Pipeline scan ──▶ parse ──▶ resolve ──▶ assemble ──▶ render ──▶ write .md HTML + link/asset SiteBundle page or 3 formats files TOC + rewriting, (JSON) page + via highlight asset bytes chunks SiteWriter pipeline::run owns the order and the side effects: Stage Input → output Module validate raw arguments + WIKICC_* environment + .wikicc.json → merged, guarded Options cli, env, options, config config input root → optional .wikicc.json → SiteConfig config scan directory + Options.exclude → ScanReport scan parse SourceDoc → HTML, TOC, plain text markdown resolve destinations → final addressing, AssetTable, diagnostics markdown::links, assets assemble everything → SiteBundle + SiteBuild site render SiteBundle → the shell page, or the shell plus one chunk per document and the search corpus render write RenderedOutput + SiteBuild → files writers Every stage except write is a pure transformation over immutable data, so it is unit tested without a filesystem. The order of the side effects is part of the contract: diagnostics are reported first, then the --strict gate runs, and only then is the page rendered and written. A build that fails on warnings therefore neither creates an artifact nor empties a previous one. 3. Module map src/main.rs binary: parse arguments, dispatch --init-config, run the pipeline, map errors to exit codes src/lib.rs library root and re-exports src/cli.rs clap definitions src/options/ the shared Settings of the CLI, the WIKICC_* environment variables and the configuration file, the three-source merge, defaults, path guards src/error.rs error type and exit-code mapping src/pipeline.rs stage order, strict gate, summary lines src/scan.rs discovery, ordering, ids, titles, diagnostics src/config.rs the optional `.wikicc.json` site configuration and its initializer src/env.rs the WIKICC_* environment variables: reading, parsing, blank-value and unknown-name policy, error messages src/favicon.rs the site favicon: the configured file, else the default embedded from docs/logo.svg at build time src/markdown/ render orchestration, heading text, slugs, TOC, chapter blocks, highlighting, link resolution, reference definitions src/assets.rs read, MIME, hashing, dedupe src/crypto.rs the seal/open primitives: PBKDF2 key derivation and AES-GCM encryption src/encrypt.rs the front-matter encrypt directive, password resolution, the sealing pass src/site.rs payload types and assembly src/render.rs shell assembly (template, CSS, script, payload), size guard src/writers/ one writer per format plus the shared placeholder expansion src/web/ page template, stylesheet and the reader's ES modules build.rs bundles src/web/js/main.js with esbuild into OUT_DIR, stages the default favicon (docs/logo.svg) into OUT_DIR, and embeds docs/logo.ico into the Windows executable tools/make-icon.mjs packs the rendered icon sizes into docs/logo.ico Dependency direction is one-way: cli → options → scan → markdown → site → render → writers → pipeline. config reads only its own file and imports options (the shared Settings) and scan (the diagnostic type), so it feeds the scan without anything reaching back into it. env reads only the process environment and imports options, so the same shape flows in from every source. markdown::links never depends on site, so link resolution stays testable on its own. 4. Invariants Rewrite the tree, not the HTML. Every document is parsed once with markdown-rs into mdast, converted to the own-layer tree, and passed through the own-layer transforms (citation fold, wikilinks, inline sugar, lenient spaced destinations, callouts) before the serialiser runs. Link and image destinations are rewritten structurally while that serialiser emits elements. Regex post-processing of HTML is rejected because attribute quoting and nesting make it unsound. One page, two addressing schemes. The document HTML is rendered once and carries an opaque placeholder (wikicc-asset:<hash>) wherever a local resource is referenced. Writers expand the placeholder into the addressing form of their format. The placeholder only ever appears inside the JSON payload — and in the shell head's single favicon link, which the writers expand with the same pass — and every substitution value is quote-free, so the payload stays valid JSON. The shell formats inline the payload; the pages format fetches. single-html and html-dir must work over file://, where fetch() of a local JSON file is blocked by CORS, so their whole payload is embedded in the page. pages is an artifact for an HTTP host: its page embeds only the manifest — one {id, title, hash} reference per document — and each document's model is one JSON file under pages/ that the reader fetches when it navigates there, with the search corpus in search.json fetched on the first global search. That format does not open from file://, and the reader says so when it finds itself there. Chunk file names derive from the document id alone, so a cached page never points at a file a redeploy removed; freshness travels in the hash, appended as a ?v= query a static host ignores but a browser counts as a new address. Assets are content-addressed. The name is the first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 digest plus the original extension, which gives free deduplication and stable names across builds and platforms. Fail soft by default. Broken links and missing assets become warnings and the original destination is left untouched; --strict upgrades them to a non-zero exit. Raw HTML passes through unchanged. The input is trusted (a local documentation folder); there is no sanitizer in this version, and this is documented rather than half-implemented. A block ends at the next heading of any level. Each body is cut into blocks — one per heading, ending where the next heading of any level starts — so every paragraph is serialised exactly once. The outline is carried on the blocks themselves (parent, subtree), which keeps aggregation a lookup rather than a walk without repeating a paragraph under every ancestor. tests/e2e.rs asserts both halves: joining a root subtree reproduces doc.html exactly, and block markup costs one body copy however deep the outline goes. Heading text has one implementation. Anchors are matched during resolution, before the target document is rendered, so the pre-pass and the renderer build heading text through the same HeadingText accumulator and the same Slugger. A chapter the build accepts is therefore a chapter the reader can reach, and the route carries the emitted slug, since only that is an element id. Static state travels in the markup. Anything the reader must know about a link that the route grammar cannot express is written into the document as data-* attributes, and every consumer reads it from there. The mark goes on an inline <span hidden> immediately before the link — the shape that stays valid inside a paragraph, a list item or a table cell, and the one the reader copies onto the anchor it points at. 5. Determinism Two builds of the same input produce byte-identical artifacts. This is a hard requirement, not an aspiration, and it constrains every stage: documents are ordered by relative path in byte order; collections that reach the output are BTreeMap/BTreeSet or explicitly sorted; assets are named after their content hash, so duplicates collapse and names do not depend on discovery order; no artifact contains a timestamp, an absolute path, a host name or a random value. The elapsed time exists only in the stdout summary; on the front end, the force layout is seeded from a hash of the document ids, the same generator feeds the initial jitter and simulation.randomSource(), and the simulation is stepped synchronously; the per-document passes — the assembly's parse/resolve work and the sealing pass — run in parallel over a worker pool, but the results are collected and merged in scan order: the thread count (jobs, default all cores) changes the wall-clock time, never the bytes. The sealing pass's random salt and nonce are the one deliberate exception — a sealed document is never byte-identical across builds, by design. 6. Contracts at the edges These are the boundaries where an internal change becomes observable, so each one is stated as a contract rather than left to the implementation. The configuration file. .wikicc.json sits in the input folder root and is optional. It carries nine keys — home, exclude, out, format, title, favicon, password, strict, jobs — exactly the Settings shape the command line and the WIKICC_* environment variables also express, and every value it names is a default: a set variable overrides it, an explicit flag overrides the variable. A relative out is resolved against the input folder (the folder the file sits in), so the build lands in the same place whatever the working directory. The file is read once, before the scan (the exclude entries must be in effect while the tree is walked; resolving home still waits for the document ids), and parsing is strict: an unreadable or unparseable file is a runtime failure, while a home that matches no document and an unknown key are warnings the --strict gate counts. The resolved id travels in the payload as home and in the pages manifest under the same key, omitted when unset, so a site without the file serialises byte-identically to a build that never heard of it. exclude lists directories relative to the input folder that are pruned with their subtrees; the pruned directories are reported as a note line, and an entry that escapes the input folder is a runtime failure, whatever the source it came from. A starter file is written by wikicc --init-config [DIR]: the default content (every key unset) goes into a directory that already exists, and a file that is already there is never overwritten. The favicon. Every page carries a favicon: the favicon setting of any source, else the wikicc logo that build.rs stages from docs/logo.svg (LF-normalized, like the page skeleton) and the binary embeds. The value is a file path relative to the input folder, normalized and guarded like the other path-shaped settings; a configured file that cannot be read is a runtime failure, because the icon is an explicit instruction. The bytes join the asset table through SiteBuild::register_favicon after assembly — deduplicated by content like every other resource, the stats growing only when the entry is new — and the rendered head addresses them by the asset placeholder the registration returns, so the writers inline a data URI in single-html and write a sibling file in the other two formats. CLI surface. cli defines the arguments; env defines the WIKICC_* variables (upper case only, blank means unset, unknown names are ignored); options owns the shared Settings (the shape all three sources express), merges the command line over the environment over the file over the built-in defaults into Options, and owns the output-directory guards (missing and empty are used, a previous artifact is emptied, anything else needs --force, and the output directory may not be the input root, its ancestor or the working directory). Three combinations are rejected before anything is written. --home and a repeatable --exclude replace the configured values, --strict is three-state — a bare flag turns the gate on, --strict=false turns it off — and --password carries the global sealing password, preferably through the WIKICC_PASSWORD variable; the password sources and the security notes live in docs/encrypt.md. --jobs caps the worker threads the parallel per-document passes run on — the count is a throughput knob only, so it never changes the bytes. Exit codes. error maps every failure to 0 (success, possibly with warnings), 1 (runtime failure, including --strict with warnings) or 2 (usage error, reported by clap). The mapping is centralised so a new stage cannot invent a code. Streams. Diagnostics go to stderr, the summary line to stdout (unless --quiet). The summary names counts, output directory, format and elapsed time — never a value that ends up inside an artifact. Testability. Everything the run prints goes through a std::io::Write sink rather than println!, so wording, gate and --quiet are unit tested without spawning a process. Formats. The three writers never re-render markup: the two shell writers share the page and differ only in asset addressing, and the pages writer expands the same placeholders into its chunk files and its shell head. A writer receives the render of its own format and refuses any other. The pages writer expands every chunk and the shell before it writes anything, writes the shell page last, so the artifact never references a file that is not on disk, and an asset-free or document-free site writes no empty directory. The payload version. Every JSON surface the reader consumes — the embedded bundle, the pages manifest, the per-document chunks and the search corpus — leads with "v": 1, the payload format version, and the reader checks it at every entry point through one helper (payload-version.js). The number bumps when a surface's shape changes in a way a reader of the previous format cannot read. A reader that finds a version it does not speak — or none — refuses the surface instead of rendering half of it: an unreadable embedded payload or manifest ends the start with a message in the article column, and a refused chunk or corpus is answered like any other failed fetch. The sealed blob's own v is the crypto format's version, checked where the blob is opened. Weight. render.rs holds a size guard that fails the build if the bundle regresses. The Windows icon. A Windows executable shows an icon in the file explorer, and that icon lives in the PE resource section. docs/logo.svg is the design source; docs/logo.ico is rendered from it and committed, so the build needs no image toolchain and stays reproducible. build.rs compiles the icon into the executable for Windows targets only, and every other target produces exactly the binary it produced before. The icon is the only thing the resource section carries, and the program keeps its console subsystem: the CLI writes to stdout and stderr as before. 7. Front end Build chain. The reader is native ES modules under src/web/js, importing the engines by bare specifier. build.rs runs the npm-installed esbuild over main.js and stages one minified IIFE in OUT_DIR, which render.rs inlines with include_str!. The page therefore has exactly one classic <script>, needs no module loader and resolves nothing at runtime. Which esbuild. node_modules/esbuild/bin/esbuild is not one kind of file: a Windows install keeps the JavaScript launcher there, while a POSIX install links the native executable of the @esbuild/<os>-<cpu> package over the same path. build.rs therefore resolves the executable the way esbuild's own install script does (an explicit ESBUILD_BINARY_PATH, then the platform package, then the installer's download, then the launcher) and executes a native binary directly, falling back to node only for a real script, so the ELF file a POSIX install leaves at the launcher path is never fed to node. Dependencies. Third-party JavaScript is ordinary npm, with exact versions in package.json and bytes pinned by package-lock.json. npm ci is a build prerequisite; a missing dependency fails the build with an actionable message instead of degrading silently. Chapter folding is a declared option of the shared body. doc-body.js owns both halves of a whole-document render, and each is the caller's declaration rather than the module's guess: the article enhances its tables, folds its chapters and arms its code blocks, the hover preview enhances the tables and folds nothing, and the search preview does none of these — the filter panel would be read as a press outside the dialog, and a fold arrow inside it would answer a click that already belongs to the list. Chapters are taken from the rendered DOM, not from the payload's outline, so a heading an author wrote as raw HTML is foldable too; a chapter runs to the next heading of the same or a higher level, so folding one covers everything nested under it. The fold state lives in the DOM alone (aria-expanded, hidden) and is never stored, so a body rebuilt for another document opens whole; a navigation into a folded chapter reopens the chapters that hold it before scrolling, because nothing scrolls to a hidden element. Code copying is a declared option of the same body. The article arms its code blocks the way it folds its chapters — the caller declares it, the previews never do — and each block is wrapped in a div that also carries the button. The wrapper takes the block's own place among the body's children, so the fold's index model is untouched and a folded chapter hides block and button together. The copy reads the code element the build emits and drops the trailing newline the build always writes, goes through the asynchronous clipboard API when the page has one, and falls back to execCommand over a selected, invisible textarea for the offline double click; a clipboard that refuses both routes changes nothing, and a copied state the button says out loud (the accent, the labels) reverts on its own a moment later. Math is typeset by the bundled KaTeX. The build emits the LaTeX source of $$…$$ blocks and $…$ spans as placeholder elements (pre.math, code.math-inline), and the reader typesets them with the engine after insertion — the same insertion-time contract as the diagrams, though the math engine needs no layout. The engine's stylesheet is staged by build.rs with every font embedded as a data URL, so the offline guarantee holds. Colours are inherited from the text, so a theme switch needs no re-render, and a formula that fails to typeset keeps its source text. Documents are looked up, then fetched. doc-store.js is the one place that knows where a document's model comes from: the payload for the shell formats, a pages/<id>.json file for the pages format. The controller renders from the store's peek when the document is on hand — every navigation of the shell formats, any revisit of the split one — and awaits get otherwise, showing a loading note and dropping the answer when a newer navigation has taken the article over. The views that need another document (the hover preview, the search panel's whole-document preview) take the store, answer synchronously from peek, and fall back to get. The search corpus of the split format is fetched once, on the first global search; the local scope reads the document in view, which is already in hand, so the default scope costs nothing. A sealed document is one more shape the store holds: decrypt is the single unlock entry, and a success replaces the cached blob with the full model and notifies the listeners — where the lock page, the search index and the preview panel all pick the article up. The hover preview never covers its link. preview-view.js places the panel below the link when the window holds it, above it when only the space over the link does, and shrunk onto the roomier side when neither side does — and every placement writes the same invariant with an inline max-height: the panel ends one gap short of the link it describes, or starts one gap past it. The height is measured once, before the placement, and the layout may disagree afterwards — a late font, a table's controls, anything the panel gains after the read — so the cap is what turns that growth into scrolling inside the body instead of the bottom edge crossing the link. tests/js/preview-view.test.js holds the invariant for all three placements, including a panel that grows after it was measured. The opening document. router.js resolves the address with one fallback chain: a known id, then the site's configured home (the payload's home key, honoured only when it names a known document), then the first document. Explicit links are never redirected; the setting only decides what an empty or unknown address opens. Layering rule. Pure logic and DOM access live in separate modules (router.js, links.js, asset-links.js, search.js, doc-store.js, lock.js, table.js, graph.js, preview.js, toc.js, anchor.js, diagrams.js, math.js versus table-view.js, graph-view.js, diagram-view.js, math-view.js, preview-view.js, search-view.js, search-highlight.js, lock-view.js, banner.js, doc-list.js), because the JS test suite runs under node --test with no DOM. Anything that touches document belongs to a view module; a view is a projection of the pure functions beneath it, and the controller (app.js) is the only module that wires views to the payload and the router. No UI framework. The reader stays on native DOM. The interactive surface is one popover plus a few attribute toggles, which does not pay for a component runtime: a framework bundle would fight the single-inline-classic- script requirement, add an output layer to the byte-identical bundle and force a DOM test environment on logic that is otherwise covered by node --test. esbuild and plain ES modules stay the whole front-end build chain. Gesture state belongs to the module that takes it. A press is recorded by the module that saw it, because the browsers and the d3 behaviours cancel every press they take, so a cancellation says nothing about ownership. A press is only ended early by a window that no longer holds the focus. One CSS custom-property set per theme. Light and dark are one declaration block switched by a root attribute; the toggle changes no other state. 8. Article encryption The scheme is specified once, in docs/encrypt.md: the front-matter directive and its strict matrix, the password sources, the AES-256-GCM parameters with their interop vectors, the reader's lock page, and the asset boundary a sealed document seals with its body. At the architecture level the feature reduces to three facts: The sealing pass is a step of assembly. encrypt.rs reads the directive out of the raw front-matter text the markdown AST carries — no second parse — and the pass runs on the assembled bundle, after the favicon registration and before the diagnostics are reported. The payload stays optional. DocModel.enc, ManifestDoc.enc and ChunkPayload.enc are skipped when unset, so a site without encryption serialises byte-identically to a build that never heard of the feature — the same determinism the whole pipeline keeps. The public surface is the reader's own metadata. A sealed document leaks its id and title alone; the search.json entry carries {id, title}, and everything else travels in the ciphertext. 9. Testing Layer Location Tooling Covers Rust unit #[cfg(test)] in each module cargo test --lib slugs, TOC, links, assets, highlighting, render, writers, options, pipeline, config, error mapping Rust integration tests/*.rs assert_cmd, tempfile, predicates CLI, scan, config, encryption, markdown, writers, end to end, the esbuild launcher build.rs picks Front-end unit tests/js/*.test.js node --test, node:assert router, search, lock, table model, graph layout, outline, preview, banner, inlined links, math policy Bridge tests/js_suite.rs Command::new("node") runs the JS suite inside cargo test Fixtures under tests/fixtures are committed sites, each pinned to one class of input; no test touches the network. The front-end dependencies are installed once with npm ci and the tests only read node_modules. Quality gates for any change: cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings, npm run check and cargo test must all pass. 10. Constraints and risks Constraint Impact Mitigation Embedded diagram engine dominates the bundle every format carries it minification plus a size guard; the engine is only initialised when the current document has a diagram Front-end dependencies are installed outside Cargo cargo build needs npm ci first build.rs fails with an actionable message; versions and bytes are pinned The npm esbuild launcher is a script on Windows and a native binary elsewhere running the launcher path through node fails on POSIX build.rs resolves the executable and starts a script with node only; a native binary runs directly file:// restrictions (CORS, module scripts) a naive SPA would break the shell formats inline the payload; the pages format requires an HTTP host and says so on a file:// page Large media in memory peak RAM during base64 encoding single-pass placeholder expansion into one reused buffer, so peak memory is the page plus one asset Raw HTML passthrough XSS if untrusted Markdown is compiled documented as trusted-input behaviour; no sanitizer No incremental build full rebuild on every run acceptable at folder scale; the artifacts are deterministic The Windows icon is a derived asset docs/logo.svg and docs/logo.ico can drift apart the icon is rendered from the source and committed, and tools/make-icon.mjs packs it deterministically; regenerating it after a design change is a documented manual step The default favicon is the embedded docs/logo.svg a changed logo changes the favicon hash of every build the staged copy is LF-normalized, so the bytes — and the hash — depend only on the committed source, never on the checkout

docs.title: Encrypted documents — how sealing works
docs.headings: Encrypted documents — how sealing works Marking a document Providing the password What stays public The reader Threat model Algorithm and parameters The build side The asset boundary Performance
docs.text: Encrypted documents — how sealing works A document can ask the build to seal it: the artifact carries the body as authenticated ciphertext, and the reader locks the article behind a password. This page describes how to mark a document, how the password travels from a build to a reader, and what stays public; the algorithm, the build-side mechanics and the boundaries of the scheme follow for reference. The product summary lives in README.md, the architecture in docs/design.md. Marking a document A document's front matter can ask the build to seal it. The key is encrypt: Front matter Meaning (no key), encrypt: false, encrypt: Build the document as usual encrypt: true Seal it with the global password encrypt: "secret" Seal it with this document's own password anything else (encrypt: "", a number, a list, invalid YAML) Fail the build with an error naming the document --- title: Private notes encrypt: true --- Nobody reads this without the password. A document with a password of its own unlocks independently of every other sealed document; encrypt: true documents share one password, so the reader never asks for the same one twice in a session. Providing the password The global password takes the same three sources as every setting, in the same order — --password over WIKICC_PASSWORD over the configuration file's password key. WIKICC_PASSWORD="opensesame" wikicc path/to/docs wikicc path/to/docs --password "opensesame" # works, but the password lands in the shell history A document that asks for encryption and finds no password anywhere fails the build: exit code 1, the error names the document on stderr, and nothing is written, whatever --strict says. There is no plaintext fallback — a build never ships a sealed declaration unsealed. Two details about the sources: A command line --password stays in the shell history and the process list, so prefer WIKICC_PASSWORD. The variable's value is trimmed, which makes the configuration file the only source that can carry a password with leading or trailing whitespace (its values are read verbatim). What stays public The title stays public. The lock page, the sidebar, the link graph and search all show the title; search reaches the body only after the reader unlocks the document — before that, a query matching the title finds a row marked Locked, and afterwards the document is ordinary (search describes the two halves). What the lock page shows is exactly what the artifact leaks: the id and the title, the same metadata the reader uses everywhere. The reader The reader shows a locked document on a lock page that carries the password field itself — the reader types where they stand, and a correct password renders the article in place. The form answers only after the reader has silently tried the passwords the session already holds, so documents sealed with one password never ask twice within a session. A reference to a sealed chapter offers the same field inside its hover preview, so the unlock happens where the reading happens. Unlocked passwords live in the session's memory alone — nothing is written to localStorage, sessionStorage or a cookie — so reloading the page relocks every document, and a fresh session asks again. Threat model The scheme protects artifacts at rest: a copied single-html file, a published pages folder, an html-dir archive — opened in a text editor they show no body, no chapter structure and no password. It does not protect the source folder — the Markdown files and the password a build was handed live in the clear on the machine that builds — and it does not protect anything against a reader who holds the password. The password is the security. The salt, the nonce and the iteration count are public parameters that weaken nothing; a short password does. Algorithm and parameters AES-256-GCM seals the body. The cipher is authenticated, so a wrong password, a wrong document binding and a tampered byte are one and the same failure, and the ciphertext layout is ciphertext || 16-byte tag — what both the RustCrypto crate and the Web Crypto API emit. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 derives the 256-bit key from the password and the salt, at 600,000 iterations (the OWASP recommendation). Per-document parameters. Every sealed document gets a fresh random 16-byte salt and 12-byte nonce at build time, so the derivation input never repeats across documents or builds. AAD binding. The document id travels as the AES-GCM additionalData, so a ciphertext cannot be transplanted into another document's blob. Plaintext shape. The sealed plaintext is the whole document model — canonical JSON {html, toc, blocks, text} — so a sealed article leaks neither body nor chapter structure; the title stays public metadata. Format version. The sealed blob leads with its own v, the crypto format's version, checked where the blob is opened. The two ends interoperate over one parameter set, pinned by fixed interop vectors committed to both test suites (src/crypto.rs and tests/js/lock.test.js): either side drifting fails both at once. file:// pages are a trustworthy context in Chrome, Edge and Firefox, so crypto.subtle is available and the scheme needs no JavaScript fallback. The build side encrypt.rs reads the encrypt field out of the raw front-matter text the markdown AST carries — extracted during the one markdown parse, no second pass — against the strict matrix above. The global password comes from the three sources in their precedence. The sealing pass runs on the assembled bundle, after the favicon registration and before the diagnostics are reported. It empties the four content fields of a sealed DocModel, writes the blob into its enc field, and leaves edges and every public metadata alone. The payload shapes stay optional: DocModel.enc, ManifestDoc.enc and ChunkPayload.enc are skipped when unset, so a site without encryption serialises byte-identically to a build that never heard of the feature, and the search.json entry of a sealed document carries {id, title} alone, so no body text reaches the browser before an unlock. The asset boundary A sealed document is self-contained. Before the body is encrypted, its own asset placeholders — in the body and in every chapter block — are expanded into data: URIs built from the asset table's MIME type and bytes, the construction the single-html writer inlines with, so the sealed body is self-contained and renders its images natively once unlocked. After all documents are sealed, the asset table is pruned to what the public documents and the favicon still address, and stats.assets and stats.asset_bytes are decremented to match: an asset referenced only by sealed documents travels inside the ciphertext and is not written to the artifact at all; an asset shared with a public document is written once, for the public reference, and the decrypted body carries its own embedded copy besides. Performance The 600,000-iteration PBKDF2 runs once per sealed document. Derivation takes seconds under an unoptimized profile, so sha2 and pbkdf2 compile at opt-level 3 in the dev and test profiles — a release build derives in milliseconds.

docs.title: Search — how to find things in the reader
docs.headings: Search — how to find things in the reader Opening the panel Typing a query Reading the results Query syntax Encrypted documents What the panel never does
docs.text: Search — how to find things in the reader The reader ships a search panel that looks through the titles, the chapter outlines and the body text of every document in the folder. This page describes how to use it and what a query means; docs/design.md describes how the reader is built. Opening the panel The panel is not on the page by default. Ask for it with the Search documents button at the top of the right-hand rail, or press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>F</kbd> (<kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>F</kbd> on macOS). It goes away again on <kbd>Escape</kbd>, on a click anywhere outside it, or when you pick a result with the field's open gesture. Typing a query Every pause in typing is a query: the results list updates as you type, about a tenth of a second after your hand stops. There is no search button to press. The scope button at the right edge of the field names the scope in force. A search starts in Local scope — the document you are reading. Pressing the button switches to Global scope, which reads every document the site holds; the choice lasts as long as the panel does. Switching the scope runs the query again at once. In the pages format the whole-site text lives in one search.json next to the page, and the first global search fetches it — once; after that the answers are as instant as they are in the other formats. Searching the document you are reading never waits: that text arrived with the document itself. The first global search shows Loading… where the results will appear, and the answer replaces it when the corpus lands. Reading the results The list shows one row per place the query is found, not one row per document: each row carries the passage around a hit, with the hit emphasised, and the file it was found in. Rows are ordered by relevance — a hit in a document's title outranks one in a chapter heading, which outranks one in the body — and the hits of one document stay together. Selecting is deliberate: click a row (or move with <kbd>↑</kbd>/<kbd>↓</kbd>, <kbd>Home</kbd>/<kbd>End</kbd>) and the preview below the list shows the whole document with every place the query occurs marked, the selected one standing out. Opening the document is a firmer gesture: double-click the row, or press <kbd>Enter</kbd>, and the reader navigates to that document at that passage — the article opens with the query's occurrences marked the same way, the passage you picked standing out. A mark covers what you typed and no more: query instal and "installation" is marked over its first six letters alone, the tail of the word left unmarked. The marks are the arrival's, not the reading's: they go when you navigate on. A row whose match is in the title or the outline alone has no passage in the body to land on; that document opens at its top. Query syntax You type What it finds bearing The whole word "bearing" and any word that begins with it ("bearings", "bearing housing"), in any case. gear ratio Documents where both words appear. Spaces separate words, and every word has to be found. 齿轮箱 The three characters consecutively, as written. A text that holds only "齿轮" elsewhere and "箱" elsewhere is not a hit. 齿 Any text holding the character — a single character is matched on its own. The rules behind the table: Case does not matter. Bearing, bearing and BEARING are the same query. A word matches whole words and their prefixes. instal finds "install", "installation" and "instalment". This applies to words written in letters and digits; there is no fuzzy matching and no wildcards. A multi-character CJK query is a phrase. Chinese (and the other Han scripts) is written without spaces, so the reader takes the characters you typed as the phrase you meant: what is found is where they appear together, in the order you typed them. To look for two separate ideas, put a space between them — 齿轮 箱体 — and each part is then matched on its own. A single CJK character is its own query. One character has no phrase to preserve, so it is found wherever it occurs, inside longer words included. Punctuation separates. Spaces, punctuation and symbols between two runs of characters break the phrase the same way a space does: gear.ratio is the two-word query gear ratio. Encrypted documents A document whose front matter asks for encryption is sealed in the artifact, and the search respects that seal: Before the unlock, only the title is searchable. The title is public — the lock page shows it — so a query that matches it produces a row marked Locked, and the preview below the list explains that the document is encrypted instead of showing a passage. Opening the row navigates to the document, which arrives on its lock page, and entering the password there renders the article. A word from the body finds nothing until the unlock. After the unlock, the document is ordinary. The same query now reaches the chapter headings and the body: rows carry their passages, the preview marks the hits, and Enter lands on the passage as always. The unlocked state lasts for the page session only — reloading the page relocks the document, and search falls back to titles alone. The build keeps the body out of the corpus entirely: in the pages format the fetched search.json names a sealed document by its title alone, so no body text reaches the browser before an unlock. What the panel never does It does not rank by position or count only: a hit in a title always leads, however early or late it sits in the body. It does not search code blocks or diagram sources for highlighting: a hit inside one is still a real result in the list, and selecting it scrolls the preview to the block that holds it, but the preview leaves those subtrees as authored so a rendered diagram is never turned back into source. Inline code — a code span inside a line of prose — is ordinary text to the highlight, and its hits are marked like any other. Rows after an unmarked hit still land on their own places — the block holds the hit's place in the order, whether or not it is marked. It does not hold on to your query: clearing the field (the clear button at the left of the scope button, or deleting the text) empties the list and the preview, and closing the panel forgets the query.
